target_customer: Enterprises and software builders that need a fast operational database for real-time ingest, analytics and applications
problem: Companies wanted to ingest, query and act on large volumes of data in real time without stitching together separate transactional and analytical systems.
business_model: Enterprise database licensing and cloud subscription, usage based

founders.name: Eric Frenkiel
founders.background_notes: YC page lists him as Founder/CEO with no bio; the company about page spells the name Erik Frankiel.

founders.name: Nikita Shamgunov
founders.background_notes: Prior employers from his YC profile; no education listed there.

founders.name: Adam Prout
founders.background_notes: Named as a founder on the company about page and Wikipedia, not on the YC page.

competitors.name: VoltDB
competitors.what: Distributed in-memory NewSQL database for OLTP
competitors.traction_then: Named by MemSQL as met in a few competitive deals

competitors.name: Clustrix
competitors.what: Clustered MySQL-compatible database on flash with no head node
competitors.traction_then: Named by MemSQL as met in a few competitive deals

technical_complexity.rationale: A distributed in-memory SQL engine with high concurrency and compiled queries is hard for a small team; the founders' infrastructure backgrounds at Facebook and Microsoft SQL Server fit the task.

defensibility.rationale: Database engines are costly to replicate and sticky once data lives in them, but buyers could pick among many databases and large vendors already sold in-memory products.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Incumbents did not buy it. SingleStore stayed independent and was taken over by a private equity buyout led by Vector Capital in 2025.

market_need_then: In 2011 the NewSQL label emerged as buyers looked for SQL databases with NoSQL scale and speed. MemSQL reported meeting VoltDB and Clustrix in deals, which shows live demand for fast distributed SQL.

branding.name_origin: MemSQL: the company said in 2020 the name signaled an in-memory SQL database. SingleStore was chosen to mean a single store for all data.

identity.logo: Not described in the sources found
identity.voice_and_tone: Product led, real-time data theme; page closes with the line All data. All in real time. All right now.

rebrands.why: Remove the impression that it is only an in-memory database and reflect a broader single store for all data

brand_strength.rationale: MemSQL was known within database circles but the company itself said the name misled buyers about the product; no sources show merch, memes or press about the brand.

outcome_analysis: MemSQL raised roughly eight venture and debt rounds from 2013 through 2022, reaching a reported valuation near 1.3 billion dollars in July 2022, and rebranded to SingleStore in October 2020 to escape the in-memory label. Growth stayed steady rather than explosive, with one third party estimate of about 123 million dollars ARR in 2025. Instead of an IPO it was sold in a growth buyout led by Vector Capital in late 2025 at an undisclosed price, which makes the exit return unknown.
notes: Directory status says Active while an acquisition by Vector Capital closed in October 2025, price undisclosed. Series A amount and investors rest on Wikipedia and an aggregator (Employbl lists IA Ventures, DCVC, Raymond Tonsing). Series D, the September 2021 and October 2022 rounds rest on Wikipedia alone; totals conflict across outlets (TechCrunch 382M in 2022, Wikipedia 318.1M) so coverage is partial. The 270M post-money for the 2018 round is a PitchBook figure quoted by TechCrunch. Competitor names come from an undated dbms2 post; its date was not verified, and DB-Engines lists VoltDB first release 2010. The 2021 round is described as a Series F in some outlets and as an extension in others; stages use series_d_plus to avoid mislabeling.
